Proof of His Desire after Them in His Having Sent Timothy: His Joy at the Tidings Brought Back Concerning Their Faith and Charity: Prayers for Them.<div eID="gen36696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17950"/><hi type="bold">1. Wherefore--</hi>because of our earnest love to you (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17-1Thess.2.20">1Th 2:17-20</reference>).<div eID="gen36697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forbear--</hi>"endure" the suspense. The Greek is literally applied to a watertight vessel. When we could no longer contain ourselves in our yearning desire for you.<div eID="gen36698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left at Athens alone--</hi>See my Introduction. This implies that he sent Timothy from Athens, whither the latter had followed him. However, the "we" favors Alford's view that the determination to send Timothy was formed during the hasty consultation of Paul, Silas, and Timothy, previous to his departure from Berea, and that then he with them "resolved" to be "left alone" at Athens, when he should arrive there: Timothy and Silas not accompanying him, but remaining at Berea. Thus the "I," <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.5">1Th 3:5</reference>, will express that the act of sending Timothy, when he arrived at Athens, was Paul's, while the determination that Paul should be left alone at Athens, was that of the brethren as well as himself, at Berea, whence he uses, <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>, "we." The non-mention of Silas at Athens implies that he did not follow Paul to Athens as was at first intended; but Timothy did. Thus the history, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.14">Ac 17:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.15">15</reference>, accords with the Epistle. The word "left behind" (Greek) implies that Timothy had been with him at Athens. It was an act of self-denial for their sakes that Paul deprived himself of the presence of Timothy at Athens, which would have been so cheering to him in the midst of philosophic cavillers; but from love to the Thessalonians, he is well content to be left all "alone" in the great city. <div eID="gen36699" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17951"/><div sID="gen36700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17951"/><hi type="bold">2. minister of God and our fellow labourer--</hi>Some oldest manuscripts read, "fellow workman with God"; others, "minister of God." The former is probably genuine, as copyists probably altered it to the latter to avoid the bold phrase, which, however, is sanctioned by <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">1Co 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2Co 6:1</reference>. The English Version reading is not well supported, and is plainly compounded out of the two other readings. Paul calls Timothy "our brother" here; but in <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:17</reference>, "my son." He speaks thus highly of one so lately ordained, both to impress the Thessalonians with a high respect for the delegate sent to them, and to encourage Timothy, who seems to have been of a timid character (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">5:23</reference>). "Gospel ministers do the work of God with Him, for Him, and under Him" [Edmunds].<div eID="gen36700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">establish--</hi>Greek, "confirm." In <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.3">2Th 3:3</reference>, God is said to "stablish": He is the true establisher: ministers are His "instruments."<div eID="gen36701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concerning--</hi>Greek, "in behalf of," that is, for the furtherance of your faith. The Greek for "comfort" includes also the idea, "exhort." The Thessalonians in their trials needed both (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1Th 3:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.14.22">Ac 14:22</reference>). <div eID="gen36702" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17952"/><div sID="gen36703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17952"/><hi type="bold">3. moved--</hi>"shaken," "disturbed." The Greek is literally said of dogs wagging the tail in fawning on one. Therefore Tittmann explains it, "That no man should, amidst his calamities, be allured by the flattering hope of a more pleasant life to abandon his duty." So Elsner and Bengel, "cajoled out of his faith." In afflictions, relatives and opponents combine with the ease-loving heart itself in flatteries, which it needs strong faith to overcome.<div eID="gen36703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yourselves know--</hi>We always candidly told you so (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.4">1Th 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.22">Ac 14:22</reference>). None but a religion from God would have held out such a trying prospect to those who should embrace it, and yet succeed in winning converts.<div eID="gen36704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we--</hi>Christians.<div eID="gen36705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed thereunto--</hi>by God's counsel (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.9">1Th 5:9</reference>). <div eID="gen36706" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17953"/><div sID="gen36707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17953"/><hi type="bold">4. that we should suffer--</hi>Greek, "that we are about (we are sure) to suffer" according to the appointment of God (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1Th 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even as--</hi>"even (exactly) as it both came to pass and ye know"; ye know both that it came to pass, and that we foretold it (compare <reference osisRef="John.13.19">Joh 13:19</reference>). The correspondence of the event to the prediction powerfully confirms faith: "Forewarned, forearmed" [Edmunds]. The repetition of "ye know," so frequently, is designed as an argument, that being forewarned of coming affliction, they should be less readily "moved" by it. <div eID="gen36708" type="x-p"/>

For this cause--</hi>Because I know of your "tribulation" having actually begun (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.4">1Th 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen36709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I--</hi>Greek, "when I also (as well as Timothy, who, Paul delicately implies, was equally anxious respecting them, compare "we," <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>), could no longer contain myself (endure the suspense)."<div eID="gen36710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I sent--</hi>Paul was the actual sender; hence the "I" here: Paul, Silas, and Timothy himself had agreed on the mission already, before Paul went to Athens: hence the "we," (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to know--</hi>to learn the state of your faith, whether it stood the trial (<reference osisRef="Col.4.8">Col 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest ... have tempted ... and ... be--</hi>The indicative is used in the former sentence, the subjunctive in the latter. Translate therefore, "To know ... whether haply the tempter have tempted you (the indicative implying that he supposed such was the case), and lest (in that case) our labor may prove to be in vain" (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.11">Ga 4:11</reference>). Our labor in preaching would in that case be vain, so far as ye are concerned, but not as concerns us in so far as we have sincerely labored (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.8">1Co 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen36713" type="x-p"/>

Our labor in preaching would in that case be vain, so far as ye are concerned, but not as concerns us in so far as we have sincerely labored ( Is 49:4 ; 1Co 3:8 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17960"/><div sID="gen36733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17960"/>11. Translate, "May God Himself, even our Father (there being but one article in the Greek, requires this translation, 'He who is at once God and our Father'), direct," &c. The "Himself" stands in contrast with "we" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.18">1Th 2:18</reference>); we desired to come but could not through Satan's hindrance; but if God Himself direct our way (as we pray), none can hinder Him (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.16">2Th 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>). It is a remarkable proof of the unity of the Father and Son, that in the Greek here, and in <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.16">2Th 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>, the verb is singular, implying that the subject, the Father and Son, are but one in essential Being, not in mere unity of will. Almost all the chapters in both Epistles to the Thessalonians are sealed, each with its own prayer (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.11">2Th 1:11</reference>; 2:16; 3:5, 16) [Bengel]. Paul does not think the prosperous issue of a journey an unfit subject for prayer (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.10">Ro 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">15:32</reference>) [Edmunds]. His prayer, though the answer was deferred, in about five years afterwards was fulfilled in his return to Macedonia. <div eID="gen36733" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17961"/><div sID="gen36734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17961"/>12. The "you" in the Greek is emphatically put first; "But" (so the Greek for "and") what concerns "YOU," whether we come or not, "may the Lord make you to increase and abound in love," &c. The Greek for "increase" has a more positive force; that for "abound" a more comparative force, "make you full (supplying 'that which is lacking,' <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.10">1Th 3:10</reference>) and even abound." "The Lord" may here be the Holy Spirit; so the Three Persons of the Trinity will be appealed to (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>), as in <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.5">2Th 3:5</reference>. So the Holy Ghost is called "the Lord" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2Co 3:17</reference>). "Love" is the fruit of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>), and His office is "to stablish in holiness" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36734" type="x-p"/>

Before not merely men, but Him who will not be deceived by the mere show of holiness, that is, may your holiness be such as will stand His searching scrutiny.<div eID="gen36736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coming--</hi>Greek, "presence," or "arrival."<div eID="gen36737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with all his saints--</hi>including both the holy angels and the holy elect of men (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">1Th 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Da 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">Zec 14:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.31">Mt 25:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7">2Th 1:7</reference>). The saints are "His" (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.13">Ac 9:13</reference>). We must have "holiness" if we are to be numbered with His holy ones or "saints." On "unblameable," compare <reference osisRef="Rev.14.5">Re 14:5</reference>. This verse (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.12">1Th 3:12</reference>) shows that "love" is the spring of true "holiness" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44-Matt.5.48">Mt 5:44-48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.10">Ro 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.14">Col 3:14</reference>). God is He who really "stablishes"; Timothy and other ministers are but instruments (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.2">1Th 3:2</reference>) in "stablishing." <chapter eID="1Thess.3"/>

God is He who really "stablishes"; Timothy and other ministers are but instruments ( 1Th 3:2 ) in "stablishing."
